A regular hexagon with side length 4 is subdivided into a lattice of 96 equilateral triangles of side length 1. Let $S$ be the set of all vertices of this lattice. Compute the number of nondegenerate triangles with vertices in $S$ that contain the center of the hexagon strictly in their interior.

message.content:
Let \(O\) be the center of the hexagon.

Use the standard cubic coordinates for the triangular lattice: lattice points are integer triples  
\[
(x,y,z)\in \mathbb Z^3,\qquad x+y+z=0,
\]
and the side-\(4\) hexagon centered at the origin is
\[
\max(|x|,|y|,|z|)\le 4.
\]
The center is \(O=(0,0,0)\). Since \(O\) itself cannot be a vertex of a triangle that contains \(O\) strictly in its interior, we only use the other \(60\) lattice vertices.

Group these vertices by the lines through \(O\). A line through \(O\) containing lattice points is generated by a primitive triple \((a,b,c)\) with \(a+b+c=0\). If
\[
m=\max(|a|,|b|,|c|),
\]
then each of the two rays of that line contains
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{4}{m}\right\rfloor
\]
lattice points.

Counting primitive directions gives:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m & \text{primitive type} & \text{number of lines} & \text{points on each ray} \\
\hline
1 & (1,-1,0) & 3 & 4 \\
2 & (2,-1,-1) & 3 & 2 \\
3 & (3,-2,-1) & 6 & 1 \\
4 & (4,-3,-1) & 6 & 1
\end{array}
\]

So there are \(18\) lines through \(O\), with ray weights
\[
4,4,4,\;2,2,2,\;\underbrace{1,1,\dots,1}_{12\text{ times}}.
\]

Now fix three distinct such lines with ray weights \(w_1,w_2,w_3\). A triangle containing \(O\) strictly cannot have two vertices on the same line through \(O\). For three distinct lines, exactly two choices of one ray from each line make the three rays surround \(O\); for any such choice, selecting one available point on each ray gives a nondegenerate triangle containing \(O\) strictly. Thus these three lines contribute
\[
2w_1w_2w_3
\]
triangles.

Therefore the desired number is
\[
2\sum_{1\le i<j<k\le 18} w_iw_jw_k.
\]

Let \(p_r=\sum w_i^r\). From the weight multiset,
\[
p_1=3(4)+3(2)+12(1)=30,
\]
\[
p_2=3(4^2)+3(2^2)+12(1^2)=72,
\]
\[
p_3=3(4^3)+3(2^3)+12(1^3)=228.
\]
Using
\[
\sum_{i<j<k} w_iw_jw_k
=\frac{p_1^3-3p_1p_2+2p_3}{6},
\]
we get
\[
\sum_{i<j<k} w_iw_jw_k
=\frac{30^3-3(30)(72)+2(228)}{6}
=\frac{27000-6480+456}{6}
=3496.
\]

Hence the number of desired triangles is
\[
2\cdot 3496=6992.
\]

\[
\boxed{6992}
\]
